questions.question_text: $y$ varies directly with $x$. When $x=8$, $y=32$. What is $y$ when $x=14$?

options.why: Used inverse variation, calculating $32(8)/14$ and rounding to $2$ decimal places.
Used $32$ as the constant of variation and calculated $32(14)$.
Added the increase in $x$, calculating $32+(14-8)$, instead of using direct proportion.

questions.solution_text: Write $y=kx$ and substitute $32=8k$. This gives $k=4$, so $y=4x$. When $x=14$, $y=4(14)=56$.

questions.question_text: $y$ varies inversely with $x$. When $x=5$, $y=36$. What is $y$ when $x=12$?

options.why: Used direct variation with $k=36/5=7.2$, then calculated $7.2(12)$.
Used $36$ as the inverse variation constant and calculated $36/12$.
Subtracted the increase in $x$, calculating $36-(12-5)$, instead of using inverse proportion.

questions.solution_text: Write $y=\frac{k}{x}$ and substitute $36=\frac{k}{5}$. This gives $k=180$, so $y=\frac{180}{x}$. When $x=12$, $y=\frac{180}{12}=15$.

questions.question_text: $y$ varies directly with $x$. When $x=9$, $y=27$. What is $x$ when $y=42$?

options.why: Multiplied $42$ by $k=3$ instead of dividing by $3$ to solve $42=3x$.
Added the increase in $y$ to the original $x$, calculating $9+(42-27)$.
Used inverse variation with $k=9(27)=243$, then calculated $243/42$ and rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.solution_text: Write $y=kx$ and substitute $27=9k$. This gives $k=3$, so $y=3x$. For $y=42$, $42=3x$, giving $x=14$.

questions.question_text: The amount of paint $P$, in litres, varies directly with area $A$, in square metres. Painting $60\text{ m}^2$ requires $6\text{ L}$. How much paint is needed for $95\text{ m}^2$?

options.why: Reversed the division for the constant, using $k=60/6=10$, then calculated $10(95)$.
Used $6$ as the constant of variation and calculated $6(95)$.
Added the increase in area to the original paint amount, calculating $6+(95-60)$.

questions.solution_text: Write $P=kA$ and substitute $6=60k$. This gives $k=0.1$, so $P=0.1A$. For $95\text{ m}^2$, $P=0.1(95)=9.5\text{ L}$.

questions.question_text:
Determine whether this table shows inverse proportion by checking the products $xy$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&2&4&8&10\\\hline y&30&15&7.5&6\\\hline\end{array}$

options.text: No; the ratios $y/x$ are not constant.
options.why: Applied the direct proportion ratio test instead of the inverse proportion product test.
Mistook the first $y$ value, $30$, for the product and omitted multiplication by $x=2$.

options.text: No; the sums $x+y$ are not constant.
options.why: Tested sums instead of the products required for inverse proportion.

questions.solution_text: The products are $2(30)=60$, $4(15)=60$, $8(7.5)=60$ and $10(6)=60$. Every pair has the same nonzero product, so the table shows inverse proportion.

questions.question_text: The time $t$, in hours, to paint a fence varies inversely with the number of painters $n$. Six painters take $10\text{ h}$. How many painters are needed to finish in $4\text{ h}$, working at the same rate?

options.why: Used direct variation, calculating $6(4)/10$, instead of inverse variation.
Added the reduction in hours to the original painter count, calculating $6+(10-4)$.
Found the constant $6(10)=60$ but did not divide it by the required time of $4$ hours.

questions.solution_text: Write $t=\frac{k}{n}$ and substitute $10=\frac{k}{6}$. This gives $k=60$, so $t=\frac{60}{n}$. For $t=4$, $4n=60$, giving $n=15$ painters.

questions.question_text: The time $t$, in hours, to clean a warehouse varies inversely with the number of cleaners $n$. Twelve cleaners take $42.5\text{ h}$. Working at the same rate, how long would $15$ cleaners take?

options.why: Used direct variation, calculating $42.5(15)/12$, instead of inverse variation.
Subtracted the extra cleaner count from the original time, calculating $42.5-(15-12)$.
Found $k=42.5(12)=510$ but did not divide by the new cleaner count of $15$.

questions.solution_text: Write $t=\frac{k}{n}$ and substitute $42.5=\frac{k}{12}$. This gives $k=510$, so $t=\frac{510}{n}$. For $15$ cleaners, $t=\frac{510}{15}=34\text{ h}$.

questions.question_text: The weight $W$, in kilograms, of a bundle of paper varies directly with the number of sheets $N$. A bundle of $600$ sheets weighs $2.7\text{ kg}$. How many sheets are in a bundle weighing $1.575\text{ kg}$?

options.why: Calculated $k$ as $0.045$ instead of $0.0045$, then divided $1.575$ by $0.045$.
Calculated $k$ as $0.00045$ instead of $0.0045$, then divided $1.575$ by $0.00045$.
Multiplied the target weight by the original sheet count, calculating $1.575(600)$, without dividing by the original weight.

questions.solution_text: Write $W=kN$ and substitute $2.7=600k$. This gives $k=0.0045$, so $W=0.0045N$. For $W=1.575$, $1.575=0.0045N$, giving $N=350$ sheets.
